question: Which statement best describes Sessions vs JWT?
options: Middleware runs at the edge before rendering and is great for CHEAP, COARSE gating (redirect unauthenticated users away from /dashboard/*) — but it should only check token presence/shape, not hit a database. Layouts and Server Components read the real session for rendering decisions (show the user's name, hide admin links). The actual authorization for a mutation belongs in the Server Action / Route Handler, not the layout.

Server Components run only on the server, so they can read the cookie and resolve the user directly with no client round-trip and no token exposure. Centralize this in one cached helper (e.g. an `auth()` function) so every Server Component, Action, and Handler resolves the user the same way and you only verify once per request.

Two ways to remember a logged-in user. A stateful SESSION stores a random opaque ID in a cookie and keeps the real data server-side (DB/Redis); it is easy to revoke but needs a lookup per request. A stateless JWT packs signed claims into the cookie itself — no lookup, but you cannot instantly revoke it and must keep it small. Most Next apps use a session cookie or a short-lived JWT plus a refresh strategy.

The session token should live in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so client JavaScript can never read it (defeating XSS token theft) and the browser attaches it automatically to same-site requests. Storing tokens in localStorage exposes them to any injected script. In Next you set this with cookies().set() in a Server Action or Route Handler.

A Server Action is a callable server endpoint — anyone who can reach the page can invoke it. So the FIRST lines of every action must re-establish identity and check permission; never trust a hidden field, the referring page, or the fact that the button was only shown to admins. Auth in the action is the real security boundary.

question: Which statement best describes Reading the session in a Server Component?
options: A Server Action is a callable server endpoint — anyone who can reach the page can invoke it. So the FIRST lines of every action must re-establish identity and check permission; never trust a hidden field, the referring page, or the fact that the button was only shown to admins. Auth in the action is the real security boundary.

Once identity is known, authorization decides WHAT they may do. RBAC attaches roles (user/editor/admin) or permissions to the session and checks them centrally — ideally one `can(user, action, resource)` helper reused by UI (to hide controls) and by every Action/Handler (to enforce). UI hiding is convenience; the server check is the gate.

Because cookies are sent automatically, a malicious site could trigger an authenticated request (CSRF). SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies block most cross-site POSTs; Auth.js also issues CSRF tokens for its forms. Server Actions are POST-only with an action-id check, which mitigates basic CSRF, but for custom cookie-auth mutations you still verify origin/SameSite and avoid GET mutations.
